title: Retrieve What’s Missing: Coverage-Maximizing Retrieval for Consistent Long Video Generation
claim: Selecting memory by greedily maximizing residual coverage of the target view fills in missing regions step by step.
layout: Top pipeline row, bottom three zoomed panels left-to-right with arrows between them
description: The figure has two tiers. The top tier is a pipeline. Historical frames pass through VGGT to produce cached depth maps. Those feed a 'Coverage-maximizing retrieval' box, which sends retrieved frames into an autoregressive diffusion model's context. The model then outputs a target frame. A funnel shape connects this box to the bottom tier. The bottom tier has three panels showing the retrieval step by step. The first panel shows temporal context frames with camera icons and a camera-trajectory sketch that includes the target pose in green, plus a grey coverage mask labeled 59% covered. The second panel (red, Retrieval 1) adds a frame and a red newly covered region, labeled 85% covered and +26 pp. The third panel (blue, Retrieval 2) adds a blue region, labeled 94% covered and +9 pp. A color legend runs along the bottom. The eye goes first to the top pipeline, then to the red and blue masks.
caption: Overview of COVRAG. During autoregressive video generation, COVRAG augments the diffusion model with retrieved historical frames that provide complementary geometric evidence for the target view. It identifies regions already supported by the temporal context and retrieves additional memories (denoted by red and blue regions) that cover the remaining target-view regions, enabling more consistent long-horizon generation. pp denotes percentage points.
abstract: Long-horizon video generation is a key capability of video world models, yet maintaining geometric consistency remains challenging. Memory-augmented generative models address this by retrieving historical frames, but their effectiveness depends on two key design choices: what 3D-geometric evidence should represent past observations, and how memory frames should be selected from this evidence. Pose-based field-of-view overlap provides lightweight but coarse geometric evidence, while explicit 3D scene memories offer finer spatial information at the cost of geometry estimation, alignment, and incremental updates over long rollouts. We propose Coverage-Maximizing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (CovRAG), a depth-based memory retrieval framework that uses pretrained 3D priors to construct a target-view coverage map as lightweight 3D memory evidence. For frame selection, CovRAG maximizes residual coverage gain, iteratively retrieving frames that explain target-view regions not covered by the temporal context or previously selected memories. To improve scalability in long-video generation, we introduce sliding-window depth caching for efficient geometry estimation. Experiments on RealEstate10K and DL3DV10K show that CovRAG improves long-horizon geometric consistency over the evaluated memory-retrieval baselines while maintaining low retrieval latency.
